turns.text: Hi, Aditya. Can you hear me clearly?
Hi, Marcus. Yes, I can hear you. Is my audio okay?
It is. There was a brief delay when you joined, but it seems stable now. If it changes, we'll pause rather than talk over the connection.
Sounds good. Thank you.

We have fifty minutes. We'll use most of it for one coding problem and a follow-up. Please clarify the prompt, talk through your reasoning, and write code in the shared editor. I'll interrupt if I need to time-box us.
Yes, that works for me.
Before we get into the main round, could you give me a brief description of yourself and what you've been working on recently?

I'm a platform engineer with experience in database migration orchestration in Go. My recent work has involved diagnosing state and performance problems under real operational constraints. I try to begin with the contract and smallest examples before selecting a data structure, and I use tests to make boundary assumptions visible rather than relying on an implementation that only works for the happy path.
What part of that project required the most careful problem solving from you personally?

In my current project on database migration orchestration in Go, I owned the problem decomposition, the core implementation, and the boundary tests for one production change. A senior reviewer challenged the rollout and another engineer handled deployment. The careful part for me was making the state invariant explicit so debugging did not depend on reading every line after an incident.
Given migration names and prerequisite pairs, return one valid execution order. Return an empty list if the dependency graph contains a cycle. Every migration name is unique.
Should I treat the input as already validated, and what are the size constraints?
There can be up to one hundred thousand migrations and three hundred thousand prerequisite pairs. A pair [A,B] means A must complete before B. Disconnected migrations are valid.
What should I return for an empty input or when there is no valid result?
Use the natural empty result for the type: zero length or an empty list. Do not throw for an ordinary no-result case.
May I use standard library collections and sorting where appropriate?
Yes. Choose the language you are comfortable with and state the operations you rely on.
Should the result be deterministic when several answers are equally valid?
Yes. Follow the tie rule in the prompt; where the prompt permits any valid result, say how your implementation behaves.

I'll restate it to make sure I have the contract. Given migration names and prerequisite pairs, return one valid execution order. Return an empty list if the dependency graph contains a cycle. Every migration name is unique. I will handle the empty case explicitly, preserve the stated tie behavior, and design for the provided upper bound rather than only the example.
Yes. That's the problem.

Let me walk a concrete case before coding. If create_users precedes add_profile and add_profile precedes backfill_profile, while create_audit is independent, either independent item can appear wherever its dependencies allow. I would also test the boundary that is most likely to change the comparison or state update.
What does that example reveal about the state you need to preserve?

It shows that I need an adjacency list, indegree map initialized for all migrations including isolated ones, a queue of ready nodes, and the result list. More importantly, the update order must preserve this invariant: every queued migration has all prerequisites emitted, indegree equals the number of unmet prerequisites, and the result never violates a directed edge. If I cannot state that before coding, it will be easy to fix one example while breaking another.
How would you start?

A direct baseline would repeatedly scan all remaining migrations for one whose prerequisites are satisfied; that can revisit the full edge set for every output node. It is useful as a correctness reference on small inputs, but it does not meet the upper bound. I would not implement it as the final answer unless the constraints were much smaller.
Can we do better under the stated constraints?

I would use Kahn's topological sort: build adjacency from prerequisite to dependent, compute indegree for each dependent, enqueue every zero-indegree migration, and decrement dependents as nodes are emitted. The reason is not only the familiar pattern: it avoids repeating work while preserving enough state to decide the next update. I will keep the implementation close to the invariant and avoid clever compression until the tests pass.
What invariant will tell you the approach is still correct as the input changes?

Every queued migration has all prerequisites emitted, indegree equals the number of unmet prerequisites, and the result never violates a directed edge. I will check it at the point where state changes, not only after the loop finishes.
What alternative did you reject, and what cost does your chosen structure introduce?

I rejected the baseline because it repeats work at the stated scale. My chosen state is an adjacency list, indegree map initialized for all migrations including isolated ones, a queue of ready nodes, and the result list, so the cost is additional memory and more careful update ordering. I accept that because it turns the dominant repeated work into bounded collection operations. If memory constraints were tighter, I would need a different contract or representation rather than pretend the state is free.
Okay. Please implement that. Keep explaining major state changes, but you don't need to narrate every character you type.
I'll take a moment to set up the function and the core state, then I'll walk through the update logic.
Talk me through the function signature and result shape before the loop.

I'll use a function that accepts the exact input and returns the requested result without mutating caller-owned data unless the prompt permits it. I handle the empty case first, initialize an adjacency list, indegree map initialized for all migrations including isolated ones, a queue of ready nodes, and the result list, and keep best-result state separate from current working state. That separation prevents a later update from corrupting the answer already found.
What happens during one normal iteration?

I read the next logical item, update the working state, then restore validity using the rule implied by the invariant. Only after the state is valid do I compare it with the best result. The core approach is Kahn's topological sort: build adjacency from prerequisite to dependent, compute indegree for each dependent, enqueue every zero-indegree migration, and decrement dependents as nodes are emitted; I will make each transition visible rather than fold it into one expression.
Why is that update order important?

If I record the answer before restoring the invariant, I can accept an invalid candidate. If I remove state too early, I can lose a valid optimum. The order follows the definition: every queued migration has all prerequisites emitted, indegree equals the number of unmet prerequisites, and the result never violates a directed edge. I am adding a short comment about why, not a comment that merely repeats the code.
What collection operation are you assuming is efficient?

The main map, set, heap, queue, or sort operations have their standard expected costs in this language. I would avoid an operation that scans or shifts a linear container inside the main loop. If the language's queue removes from the front of an array in linear time, I would use an indexed head or a real deque.
Pause and inspect the boundary comparisons in what you wrote.

I see the main risk. The implementation currently increments indegree on the prerequisite instead of the dependent because the pair direction is read backward. That may pass the central example but violates the stated boundary rule. I want to construct the smallest counterexample before I change it so the correction is evidence-driven.
Use that counterexample. What state changes?

On the counterexample, the current code leaves state that should have been updated or evicted. The correct action is to name the tuple fields prerequisite and dependent, add the edge prerequisite to dependent, and increment indegree of dependent; then verify the smallest two-node example. I'll change that line and keep the counterexample as a named test rather than only testing it mentally.
Continue. How do you produce the result without disturbing correctness?

After the main processing finishes, I convert the maintained best state to the requested return format. If reconstruction is required, I do it iteratively where input depth could be large. I keep deterministic tie behavior in one comparison helper so it is not implemented differently in two places.
Do you need to handle malformed input?

The prompt says ordinary inputs satisfy the stated contract, so I won't spend interview time on a full validation layer. I will handle empty or no-result cases that are part of the domain. In production I would validate external input at the boundary and decide whether malformed data is rejected, quarantined, or logged; that is separate from the algorithm.
Read the code once from the invariant's perspective.

Initialization makes the invariant true for an empty prefix. Each iteration updates the new item, restores validity, and records the best state only afterward. The final result comes from state that was valid when recorded. The remaining uncertainty is the exact boundary in the correction, so the next tests should target that before broad random cases.
Before you type further, give me language-neutral pseudocode.

The pseudocode is: validate the ordinary empty case; initialize an adjacency list, indegree map initialized for all migrations including isolated ones, a queue of ready nodes, and the result list; iterate through the input in its required order; update the working state; restore or verify the invariant; compare the valid candidate with the best using the tie rule; and reconstruct or format the answer after processing. The problem-specific update is Kahn's topological sort: build adjacency from prerequisite to dependent, compute indegree for each dependent, enqueue every zero-indegree migration, and decrement dependents as nodes are emitted. Writing this first makes it easier to see whether the code changes the order of two logically separate operations. For this problem, I would verify that reasoning specifically against the graph modeling requirement.
Give me a short correctness argument, not only intuition.

For initialization, the working state represents the empty processed prefix, so the invariant holds. For maintenance, one iteration adds the next item and applies the exact correction needed to restore this invariant: every queued migration has all prerequisites emitted, indegree equals the number of unmet prerequisites, and the result never violates a directed edge. We record an answer only while that invariant holds. At termination every input item has been considered, and any candidate that could beat the result was represented when its decisive boundary was processed. The tie comparison preserves the required deterministic choice. For this problem, I would verify that reasoning specifically against the topological sort requirement.
Trace the central example through the actual variables you wrote.

I start with the empty state and process the example one item at a time: If create_users precedes add_profile and add_profile precedes backfill_profile, while create_audit is independent, either independent item can appear wherever its dependencies allow. At each point I would say the current state, whether the invariant is valid, and whether the best result changes. The important trace is the transition that removes, evicts, advances, or reconstructs state; that is where the first implementation was most likely to diverge from the algorithm I described. For this problem, I would verify that reasoning specifically against the cycle detection requirement.
How are you enforcing the tie rule in code?

I use one helper that answers whether a new candidate is better than the stored result. It compares the primary score first and only then the specified deterministic tie field. I do not rely on map iteration, heap incidental order, or sort stability unless the language contract guarantees it and the prompt accepts that behavior. A named helper also gives me a direct unit test at the tie boundary. For this problem, I would verify that reasoning specifically against the failure return requirement.
What input ownership or mutation assumption does your code make?

I will not mutate caller-owned input unless the interface explicitly allows it. If sorting is part of the algorithm, I either copy first or state that in-place sorting is part of the contract. Collections inside the function are local. In production I would also consider memory cost of a copy against API clarity; in an interview, silently changing input creates a surprising side effect and makes later tests order-dependent. For this problem, I would verify that reasoning specifically against the graph modeling requirement.
How would you use randomized or property testing here?

I would generate small valid inputs, compare the optimized answer against the simple baseline that would repeatedly scan all remaining migrations for one whose prerequisites are satisfied; that can revisit the full edge set for every output node, and assert structural properties such as determinism, valid indices or order, and the invariant. Small random cases are effective at exposing boundary combinations I did not name. They complement, not replace, targeted tests for the exact bug and product rule. For this problem, I would verify that reasoning specifically against the topological sort requirement.
Is there an integer, recursion, or allocation risk at the upper bound?

I would use a numeric type large enough for counts and derived totals, avoid recursive depth proportional to the input, and ensure the inner loop does not create a new substring, array, or object on every step without need. Output allocation is unavoidable where the result itself is large. I would measure before micro-optimizing, but the upper bound is large enough that asymptotically hidden allocation matters. For this problem, I would verify that reasoning specifically against the cycle detection requirement.
If memory became the primary constraint, what would you revisit?

I would first separate memory required for an exact answer from convenient implementation state. The current method retains an adjacency list, indegree map initialized for all migrations including isolated ones, a queue of ready nodes, and the result list. Some of that can be compressed using indices, integer IDs, packed arrays, or an output-sensitive structure. If the exact contract fundamentally requires state proportional to distinct items or discovered nodes, I would say so and discuss approximation, external storage, or a changed API rather than claim constant space. For this problem, I would verify that reasoning specifically against the failure return requirement.
How would this function fail observably in production?

I would expose input size, latency, allocation or queue growth where relevant, result cardinality, and counts of invalid or no-result outcomes. I would not log entire sensitive inputs. A rollout could compare the optimized implementation with the trusted baseline on sampled small cases or shadow traffic. If disagreement occurs, retain the stable request identifier and enough bounded state to reproduce it. For this problem, I would verify that reasoning specifically against the graph modeling requirement.
I think there is a case where the code increments indegree on the prerequisite instead of the dependent because the pair direction is read backward. Can you find it without me giving the input?

Yes. The smallest counterexample is one that lands exactly on that boundary or requires the state to change twice. Walking it line by line, the code preserves an invalid or incorrectly ordered state. The root issue is that it increments indegree on the prerequisite instead of the dependent because the pair direction is read backward; it is not a syntax problem.
Make that change in the code, then let's test it.

I've updated it to name the tuple fields prerequisite and dependent, add the edge prerequisite to dependent, and increment indegree of dependent; then verify the smallest two-node example. I also separated the boundary comparison into a named condition so the product rule is readable. I'll rerun the counterexample first, then the original sample, because fixing the edge should not change the normal path.
Test 1: no migrations. What do you expect?

For no migrations, I would state the exact expected result, walk only the state transition that is different, and verify both the returned value and the relevant tie or parent behavior. This case exists because it can break an assumption that the central sample does not exercise.
Test 2: one isolated migration. What do you expect?

For one isolated migration, I would state the exact expected result, walk only the state transition that is different, and verify both the returned value and the relevant tie or parent behavior. This case exists because it can break an assumption that the central sample does not exercise.

For multiple disconnected components, I would state the exact expected result, walk only the state transition that is different, and verify both the returned value and the relevant tie or parent behavior. This case exists because it can break an assumption that the central sample does not exercise.

For a two-node cycle, I would state the exact expected result, walk only the state transition that is different, and verify both the returned value and the relevant tie or parent behavior. This case exists because it can break an assumption that the central sample does not exercise.

What are the time and space costs of the final version?
O(V plus E) time and O(V plus E) space for adjacency, indegrees, queue, and result. I am including input, output, and maintained state rather than quoting only the loop cost.
Return the lexicographically smallest valid order when several migrations are ready.

Replace the FIFO ready queue with a min-heap keyed by migration name. Correctness is unchanged; selecting the smallest currently available node gives the lexicographically smallest topological order. Time becomes O((V plus E) log V) in the worst case because heap operations are logarithmic.
What guarantee becomes weaker or what cost becomes larger in that follow-up?

The original correctness argument still applies only where the contract is unchanged. I would explicitly document the new memory, ordering, or approximation cost and add a test that distinguishes it from the original version. I would not silently present a heuristic as the same exact solution.
I have what I need. What questions do you have for me?
How does this team evaluate a candidate who has the right reasoning but does not finish every line of code?

We score problem framing, correctness of the chosen approach, communication, code quality, and testing separately. An incomplete but coherent solution can still show useful signal; silent guessing usually does not.
That's helpful. I prefer making the tradeoffs visible rather than hiding unfinished work.
What kind of problems would an engineer at this level own after joining?
The team owns schema and migration orchestration and expects engineers at this level to deliver bounded changes through testing and production follow-up.
That scope sounds appropriate.
Those were my main questions. Thank you for the context and for your time.
I need to finish my notes and compare them with the rest of the interview team, so I won't give feedback on this call. The recruiter will contact you about the next step within a few business days.
Understood. Thank you, Marcus. Have a good day.
You too, Aditya. Take care.
